verification.note: Complete signed one-page essay read in all three columns, printed 6/PDF leaf 6, from the original magazine publisher’s archive; page visually collated against OCR. Opening editorial introduction remains distinct from Wedgwood’s own testimony. Her strongest debts to Schiller, Burckhardt, Trevelyan, Neale and Canetti are explicit missing-endpoint holds. Bloch acknowledgment identifies no particular work or doctrine; no listed historian’s original work newly read. Remaining magazine pages unread.

sources.citation: Lawrence Stone, “History à la Mode,” New York Review of Books, 10 September 1964, review of C. V. Wedgwood, A Coffin for King Charles (Macmillan, 1964).

verification.note: Complete displayed signed review read in original publisher HTML, from “In January 1649” to the final sentence about a weightier cause. Praise for narrative skill coexists with political, methodological and evidentiary criticism. Stone’s judgments and historical claims remain attributed; the book, archival material and unidentified earlier critic he quotes were not independently read. No reply by Wedgwood located in the bounded publisher search.

wedgwood_woolrych.note: Complete original British Academy memoir 521–534 freshly read, including all 14 notes, with title/portrait leaf distinct. Existing seminar, advice, revaluation, Parker criticism, biographical caveats and cultural placements remain intact. Schiller’s and Trevelyan’s stronger personal roles are freshly supported by Wedgwood’s own 1960 essay; the memoir alone does not newly establish Bloch’s role. The 1986 Festschrift contributor list does not prove shared doctrine or influence; Woolrych’s 528 polemic is not assigned to Wedgwood. Original prefaces, Parker’s 1984 book and the original 1958 art/science essay remain unread.
